studies.finding: The selected dried Fe-gluconate specimen has a broad XRD pattern classified as amorphous, in contrast with the crystalline hydrated parent specimen. Fe-57 velocity-dependent transmission spectra show resonant attenuation at finite absorber temperatures across the reported 78-295 K study; Figure 2 displays 78 K and 268 K examples. This is a positive bound-solid Mossbauer case whose absorber is not reported to possess perfect periodic crystal order. The three-doublet analysis yields finite widths and distinct center shifts and quadrupole splittings under the stated spectral model. At 295 K its normalized area quantities a1,a2,a3 are 0.49,0.46,0.52 relative to 78 K. The model-derived effective Debye temperatures differ: Table 2 reports 377(9) K from CS1 and 204(4) K from a1. These results illustrate finite-temperature spectral and vibrational sensitivity, with fitted hyperfine/electronic-environment interpretation, rather than a natural-width measurement or absolute recoilless probability.
limitations: This is one primary experiment context containing sample X-ray characterization and finite-temperature transmission spectroscopy. Its spectra, fitted components, relative areas and Debye interpretations share the same specimen/measurements; they are not independent replications.

The measured sample is powdered Fe-gluconate prepared by dissolution and drying at 50 degrees C. XRD-amorphous is the reported finite-sensitivity diffraction classification, not proof that every atomic neighborhood has no order.

The source reports about 10 mg Fe per cm^2, 1024 channels, source at room temperature, 78-295 K absorber range and temperature stability within plus/minus 0.1 K. These preparation/control values are not error bars on fitted shifts or proof of the thin-absorber approximation for every material.

The quoted typical Table 1 errors are source estimates, without a reconstructed confidence convention or complete covariance/systematic budget. No raw counts, background, thickness correction, calibration fit or independent uncertainty replay was obtained.

The earlier crystalline comparison study and imported Debye/isomer-shift references are not separately reviewed or admitted as additional studies. The original 1959 paper was not obtained as actual article text; a seven-page anthology contents PDF is not that article.

The XRD classification and transmission profiles establish a finite observed case; they do not measure a universal ordering threshold, a unique local coordination geometry or an exactly absent crystalline volume fraction.
Figure 2 displays 78 K and 268 K examples. The study range reaches 295 K; the plotted higher-temperature example must not be relabelled 295 K.

The fitted D1,D2,D3 curves are model components overlaid on measured spectra. Their existence as a useful decomposition does not alone establish three unique phases, three distinct atom positions or an independent magnetic-ordering measurement.
The transmission scale is relative; no new absolute absorption cross section, absolute gamma-emission probability, natural linewidth or independent f measurement is inferred.

Table 1 center shifts are relative to the Co-57/Rh source at room temperature, not automatically to metallic alpha-Fe. Its shift, splitting and full-width-at-half-maximum entries are in mm/s; the fitted widths are not natural nuclear energy widths.

At 295 K the table lists a1,a2,a3 as 0.49,0.46,0.52 after normalization to unity at 78 K. These are relative normalized spectral-area quantities under the stated approximation, not absolute probabilities f(295 K).

studies.finding: Close to the orifice the diffraction profiles show the broad main peak of the disordered liquid; with increasing distance the diffuse liquid scattering decreases while five sharp peaks rise and dominate, identified as the (111), (200), (220), (311) and (222) reflections of the fcc structure into which rare-gas liquids crystallize. The jets crystallize spontaneously by homogeneous nucleation into solid filaments; the fraction crystallized rises to about 0.75 within about 25 microseconds for pure argon and to about 0.6 within about 20 microseconds for pure krypton, with Avrami exponents close to 1. The x = 0.4 mixture crystallized about five times more slowly than the pure jets; onset temperatures followed T(x) = 74.7 + 28.7x K, and the composition dependence of the growth rates was accounted for only after scaling the collision-limited addition rate by the thermodynamic non-ideality factor.
limitations: The source treats the rare gases as Lennard-Jones systems; the interatomic attraction is not measured here.
